title: 'Count Your Days': Labor Department Escalates H-1B Fraud Hunt Beyond Tech
excerpt: The DOL inspector general says whistleblower tips are feeding a nationwide probe into visa mills, wage kickbacks and labor trafficking, with Cognizant and Cloudera facing suspended filings.
body:
• The Labor Department's Office of Inspector General is ramping up a nationwide probe into H-1B and PERM fraud, with IG Anthony D'Esposito posting a blunt warning on X: "Count your days."
  • The investigation covers "visa mills," wage kickbacks, labor brokers, benching of foreign workers and possible human trafficking — now beyond tech, including healthcare.
  • Cognizant and Cloudera have had PERM filings suspended; the Labor Department in May halted Cloudera's PERM processing for 180 days after DOJ evidence it shut out US workers.
  • D'Esposito says whistleblower tips from inside big companies are feeding the probe, and the OIG has issued dozens of subpoenas alongside the White House fraud task force.

The Trump administration's scrutiny of the H-1B visa program is widening. The Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General said a growing number of whistleblower complaints and public tips are feeding a nationwide investigation into suspected fraud and abuse — and the watchdog's message to alleged fraudsters was blunt: "Count your days."

In a post on X on Wednesday, the OIG said information from whistleblowers, members of the public and investigators was feeding its work with the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud. Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito told Fox News there is "without a doubt" fraud happening, citing tips from whistleblowers inside large companies.

Investigation expands beyond technology

The probe covers alleged fraud in the H-1B and PERM programs, including fraudulent applications, wage-related kickbacks, labor brokers and potential human trafficking. Crucially, D'Esposito said the investigation is no longer confined to the technology industry — healthcare and other sectors are being examined too.

The OIG investigates employers, immigration lawyers and labor brokers across several foreign-worker programs, including H-1B, H-2A, H-2B and PERM, the latter being the labor certification employers must clear before sponsoring workers for green cards.

Field inspections turn up empty offices

The watchdog has moved beyond desk reviews. During an August visit to Dallas, investigators checked addresses tied to companies with hundreds of approved H-1B petitions. At one multi-office property linked to more than 500 approved petitions, several offices appeared inactive — locked doors, lights switched off.

"This isn't just paperwork fraud — it's the exploitation of vulnerable workers, forced labor, the displacement of American workers, and abusive human trafficking," D'Esposito said in a July statement, when the nationwide enforcement initiative launched alongside Vice President J.D. Vance's anti-fraud task force.

Big names under scrutiny

The crackdown has reached marquee employers. D'Esposito announced that PERM filings by Cognizant — founded in Chennai in 1994 and now headquartered in New Jersey — have been suspended, writing on X that "Fighting fraud is a TEAM SPORT" and "Handcuffs await." Cognizant had 3,510 H-1B petition approvals as of June 30, down from 9,413 in 2020.

Separately, in May the Labor Department suspended processing of all PERM applications filed by or for Cloudera for 180 days, after Justice Department evidence showed the company had built a recruitment process that prevented qualified US workers from applying for certain technology positions. The DOJ subsequently sued.

"Threats to American workers will NOT be tolerated."

— Anthony D'Esposito, Labor Department Inspector General

Context & Background

The push is part of Project Firewall, a multi-agency initiative launched in September 2025 to increase H-1B oversight. Since then the Labor Department has opened more than 175 investigations. A shift to "Secretary-certified" audits lets the Labor Secretary personally initiate audits on "reasonable cause" alone — a lower threshold than before — and companies can face unannounced site visits, civil penalties and even criminal charges.

Diaspora Angle

Indians are the largest H-1B beneficiary group by far, and India-founded firms like Cognizant sit directly in the probe's path — so even compliant workers could face slower filings, employer audits and renewed paperwork as scrutiny cascades down.

What's Next

D'Esposito says dozens of subpoenas are already out and every lead will be tracked. With 175-plus investigations open and whistleblower rewards on the table, more employers — across more industries — are likely to be named.
